newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Heart surgeon cuts through Kremlin secrecy.
newsitem.headline: Heart surgeon cuts through Kremlin secrecy.

text.p: Renat Akchurin, the cardiologist leading heart bypass surgery on President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday, landed himself a temperamental patient who was a lot sicker than anyone had let on.

With quiet insistence, courage and professionalism, Akchurin, one of Russia's leaders in the field, cut through the veil of secrecy woven by the Kremlin and persuaded the 65-year-old president to take his illness seriously.
In doing so he saved Yeltsin -- who he has compared to a difficult child -- and himself, from an early operation which could have ended in disaster.

Akchurin, 50, is not the first surgeon asked to perform miracles to preserve the facade that Kremlin leaders' health never fails. But he seems to be the first to have got away with publicly disputing the official line.

On September 20, more than a fortnight after Yeltsin said he would have a simple heart operation and as clocks ticked towards the date Yeltsin had given for surgery, Akchurin turned to the media for a way out of the corner into which he had been led.

Saying he had got no green light from the Kremlin, he dropped the bombshell that Yeltsin had suffered a third, hitherto unreported, heart attack right before he was re-elected president in July, and that it might be wise to delay surgery.
Doctors met days later and agreed that the president should spend another six weeks getting ready for the operation, which was eventually performed on November 5.

Akchurin added a quiet reprimand for those who tried to play down the illness. "Such a serious operation, albeit performed on hundreds of thousands of people in the world, should not be presented as elementary," he told Russian television.
Akchurin criticised Yeltsin for driving himself too hard in his campaign for re-election and then going hunting when he was supposed to be resting.
"Boris Nikolayevich, I'm not afraid to repeat it, is a difficult patient...There are difficult children as you know. As for Boris Nikolayevich, he is a difficult patient," he said.

Akchurin, born in the then-Soviet republic of Uzbekistan, heads the cardiovascular surgery department at the Cardiology Research Centre of academician Yevgeny Chazov -- who was in charge of treating the Soviet elite for 23 years.
Akchurin has had his share of famous patients. He operated on Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin eight years ago and has also done a bypass for Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Lobov.
He has said he owes much to pioneering U.S. cardio-surgeon Michael DeBakey, who trained him in the United States in 1984, and asked him for advice in his treatment of the president.
Akchurin refers to DeBakey as a father figure and in typically-Russian literary style "the Leo Tolstoy of cardiovascular surgery".

The 88-year-old U.S. workaholic passed on to Akchurin the coronary bypass technique he had pioneered -- using vein tissue to create an alternative blood passage around constricted arteries near the heart.
Since then Akchurin said he had done about 100 operations a year in the centre, equipped with Western-made instruments. He says his record is comparable to top U.S. clinics.
Akchurin said he was confident that plans to delay Yeltsin's surgery had raised the chances of success to close to 100 percent from 80 percent at the end of September.
Having made it clear to everyone what he was up against, he insisted, convincingly, that he was not afraid.
"I am aware of my responsibility. But...I know that all hearts are the same."
